newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia protestors rally, violence erupts in Kosovo.
newsitem.headline: Serbia protestors rally, violence erupts in Kosovo.

text.p: Pro-democracy demonstrators kept up pressure on Serbia's beleaguered President Slobodan Milosevic on Saturday while communal tensions mounted in the tinder box region of Kosovo.

Reports that Serbian police shot dead three ethnic Albanians, including a suspected Kosovo guerrilla, and footage on state television showing arms allegedly seized in Kosovo underlined fears of a revival of sectarian unrest.

In Belgrade, thousands of students, unimpeded by police, tramped across a Sava river bridge and circled a shopping complex to express their disapproval of a state-sponsored film festival that opened in the capital on Friday.

Separately, about 60,000 supporters of the Together opposition alliance converged after dark on Republic Square for the 77th straight day of protests demanding Milosevic reinstate opposition victories in local elections on November 17.

Milosevic's ruling socialists have appeared increasingly divided and uncertain, with teachers on strike, more than 1,000 schools shut, university deans in open revolt against government-appointed rectors and lawyers rallying for democratic reform.

The crisis has hit investor confidence. The British banking group National Westminster Plc said on Friday it had withdrawn as adviser to the federal Yugoslav government on negotiations with the Balkan state's international creditors.

Yugoslavia is waiting to begin talks with the International Monetary Fund and World Bank on repaying $1.3 billion. It needs to agree terms before it can get new loans desperately needed to rebuild an economy exhausted by the war in Bosnia.
The official Yugoslav new agency Tanjug reported that a suspected commander of the shadowy Liberation Army of Kosovo was among three men killed in a gunbattle with Serbian police on Friday.
Quoting the Serbian Interior Ministry, it said the police were shot at by the men in a car and returned fire. Three police officers were wounded.
Serbian state television showed what it said were automatic rifles, ammunition, explosive and maps of state buildings seized in police raids in Kosovo over the past week.
It described the three ethnic Albanians as outlaws and said weapons were found in the car in which were travelling.
But Kosovo's main political party, which represents ethnic Albanians, condemned the police killings as part of a brutal Serbian crackdown and it appealed to the international community for help.

The Democratic League said the shooting followed a series of violent police raids on the homes of Albanians. It said dozens of humanitarian workers and political activists had been detained and some of them had been beaten and tortured.
Milosevic took away Kosovo's autonomy status in 1989, maintaining that the majority ethnic Albanians were preparing to secede.
Western political analysts have sinve viewed the region as a flashpoint that could plunge the Balkans into a fresh paroxysm of communal bloodshed.

Mainstream ethnic Albanian politicians have tried to distance themselves from the marathon Serbian protests against Milosevic for fear of being used as a possible scapegoat by the increasingly-isolated socialist leadership.
Little is known of the Kosovo Liberation Army, although it has claimed several attacks over the past year in which both Serbians and ethnic Albanians were killed.
